newsitem.title: JORDAN: Israel cancels gas joint venture with Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Israel cancels gas joint venture with Jordan.

text.p: Israel has formally pulled out of a joint venture with Jordan to set up a $300 million gas plant in Jordan that would have supplied the two countries with gas from the Gulf, Jordanian officials said on Sunday. "The project is

non-existent...the new Israeli government is apparently not interested in the project any longer," Energy Minister Hashem Dabbas told Reuters, adding that Israel had probably opted for other sources of gas.

The deal was agreed at a Middle East economic summit two years ago amid a wave of optimism about Arab-Isreali economic cooperation. But Israel's enthusiasm for the project appeared to wane in the following months.

U.S. energy giant Enron Corp spearheaded the project to set up a $300 million regasification plant at Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba to bring liquefied natural gas (LNG) from the Gulf state of Qatar to Israel and Jordan in the first quarter of 2001.

Investors say the Israeli government's reluctance was based on economics. They say Israel believes getting LNG from Qatar by vessels was more expensive than other sources including direct pumping of gas from Egypt.
Israel's previous Labour government strongly lobbied for the project, despite opposition of some Israeli industrial groups, to help draw Jordan closer economically and consolidate peace.
The project grew out of an initial understanding between Enron and Israel reached in October 1995 in Amman for the supply of at least two million tonnes of Qatari gas to Israel.

Originally Israel was to get an estimated 75 percent of gas and Jordan the remaining 25 percent. The plant was to have taken two years to construct with the first Qatari gas deliveries to Jordan and Israel by the first quarter of the year 2001.
Dabbas said that Jordan's own letter of intent with Enron signed last March also lapsed after a 180-day period expired.
Investors say the project collapsed after Israel and Jordan failed to finalise long-term supply accords with Enron.
Jordanian investors said Enron had been notified by Israel late last year that it no longer was interested in the project.
"The Israeli government sent a letter to Enron saying that a letter of intent it signed with Enron in October 1995 was no longer binding," said an investor close to the deal.
Dabbas, however, said that Enron still had not shelved plans to set up a electric power plant in Aqaba, part of its original plan for the regasification plant.
Bureaucratic delays on the Jordanian side after Enron chose a site in Aqaba and financing problems had already added to the project's complications, investors said.

The joint venture company in which Jordanian and Israeli investors were to hold an equal 25 percent equity share with Enron holding a 50 percent was formally registered in Jordan and Israel but never capitalised, investors said.
The project was the largest undertaking planned so far between the Israeli and the Jordanian private investors since a peace treaty in 1994 that ended a 46-year state of war.
Investors say its collapse is a serious setback to efforts to create large private sector joint ventures between the two states that would create a common interest in preserving peace.
Smaller scale Israeli-Jordanian business ventures have been in the pipeline but the slow pace of progress in Middle East peace hindered their implementation, investors say.
